body: INSERT statements that dont use RETURNING do not need to use insertmanyvalues.  an exception is made for psycopg2 because it has extremely slow executemany() performance that is unique to that driver.

rename.from: Rowcount returns -1 in pycopg3 insert. Also insertmanyvalues is not used.
rename.to: Rowcount returns -1 in pycopg3 insert without returning

It's quite strange, adding returning makes the rowcount work in pg3. This looks like something strange is going on on pg3 for some reason.
```py
import psycopg
import psycopg2
import sqlalchemy as sa

url = "postgresql://scott:tiger@localhost/test"

def using_sqlalchemy_returning(mod, echo):
    if mod == "psycopg2":
        url_driver = url.replace("postgresql", "postgresql+psycopg2")
    else:
        url_driver = url.replace("postgresql", "postgresql+psycopg")
    e = sa.create_engine(url_driver)
    e.connect().close()
    e.echo = echo
    t = sa.Table("tbl", sa.MetaData(), sa.Column("col", sa.Integer))
    with e.connect() as con:
        t.create(con)
        res = con.execute(
            t.insert().values([{"col": i} for i in range(1, 4)]).returning(sa.literal(1))
        )
        print(mod, "insert values", res.rowcount)
        res = con.execute(
            t.insert()
            .from_select(
                ["col"],
                sa.func.generate_series(2, 7).table_valued("col").render_derived("t").select(),
            )
            .returning(sa.literal(1))
        )
        print(mod, "insert select", res.rowcount)
        res = con.execute(t.insert().returning(sa.literal(1)), [{"col": 8}, {"col": 9}])
        print(mod, "insert values exec many", res.rowcount)

        con.rollback()

print("sqlalchemy returning")
using_sqlalchemy_returning("psycopg2", echo=False)
using_sqlalchemy_returning("psycopg", echo=False)
```

ok this seems to come from psycopg, basically the usage in sqlalchemy is as follows:
```py
import psycopg
import psycopg2
import sqlalchemy as sa

url = "postgresql://scott:tiger@localhost/test"

def using_driver(mod):
    if mod == "psycopg2":
        con = psycopg2.connect(url)
    else:
        con = psycopg.connect(url)
    with con:
        with con.cursor() as c:
            c.execute("create table tbl (col int)")
        with con.cursor() as c:
            c.execute("insert into tbl values (1), (2), (3)")
        print(mod, "insert values", c.rowcount)
        with con.cursor() as c:
            c.execute("insert into tbl values (1), (2), (3) returning 1")
        print(mod, "insert values returning", c.rowcount)
        with con.cursor() as c:
            c.execute(
                "insert into tbl select t from "
                "generate_series(%s::int,%s::int) as t ",
                (5, 9),
            )
        print(mod, "insert select params", c.rowcount)
        with con.cursor() as c:
            c.executemany("insert into tbl values (%s)", [(8,), (9,)])
        print(mod, "insert values exec many", c.rowcount)
        con.rollback()

using_driver("psycopg2")
using_driver("psycopg")
```

this prints the same as sqlalchemy:

```
driver
```

I'm guessing that the current behavior of psycopg3 is by design. Gonna ask

**Federico Caselli** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **main** branch:

**Save rowcount in an insert before the cursor is closed** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/5153

tried in other driver backends what is populated in the rowcount after an insert:
- pg8000 is like psycopg2
- asyncpg like psycopg2 expect for executemany
- sqlite like psycopg2
- mssql like psycopg2 execpt for returning (it's -1 there)
- oracle like psycopg3 (always -1 but returning)

```py
import asyncio
import psycopg
import psycopg2
import sqlalchemy as sa
import sqlalchemy.util

url = "postgresql://scott:tiger@localhost/test"

def using_sqlalchemy_conn(mod, echo):
    url_driver = url.replace("postgresql", f"postgresql+{mod}")
    e = sa.create_engine(url_driver)
    e.connect().close()
    e.echo = echo
    t = sa.Table("tbl", sa.MetaData(), sa.Column("col", sa.Integer))
    with e.connect() as con:
        t.drop(con, checkfirst=True)
        t.create(con)
        if 'oracle' in url_driver:
            res = con.execute(t.insert().values({"col": 1}))
        else:
            res = con.execute(t.insert().values([{"col": i} for i in range(1, 4)]))
        print(mod, "insert values", res.rowcount)
        res = con.execute(t.insert().from_select(["col"], t.select()))
        print(mod, "insert select", res.rowcount)
        res = con.execute(t.insert(), [{"col": 8}, {"col": 9}])
        print(mod, "insert values exec many", res.rowcount)
        res = con.execute(
            t.insert().returning(sa.literal(1)), [{"col": 8}, {"col": 9}]
        )
        print(mod, "insert values exec many returning", res.rowcount)

        con.rollback()
```

Also re-reading the rowcount definition in [pep-249](https://peps.python.org/pep-0249/#rowcount):

> This read-only attribute specifies the number of rows that the last produced (for DQL statements like SELECT) or affected (for DML statements like UPDATE or INSERT)

I think that sqlalchemy usage of rowcount is a bit limited, since it says only update and delete, while the pep also mention insert
https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/core/connections.html#sqlalchemy.engine.CursorResult.rowcount

So I would propose to expand the sqlalchemy support to also include inserts.

@zzzeek Do you remember why insert was excluded? I see only mentioned that in case of a select it's not accurate
most drivers dont work correctly here with inserts so we can't really say it's "supported".

not to mention with inserts we switch so often between execute() and executemany() based on many transparent factors, it does not seem possible to get "rowcount" to be at all predictable across statements themselves, never mind drivers

At the dev meeting was decided to try to add an execution option `preserve_rowcount=True` that would memoize in all cases the rowcount of the driver.

This would also sum up the various rowcounts when performing an executemanyvalues
